 Texas food recalls: FDA only inspects 900 of 19,200 foreign food plants
 A federal watchdog found food safety inspections falling far short of what the law requires. A Houston rancher, state investigators, and a summer of outbreaks show what’s at stake.
 Brandon Walker , Investigative Reporter
 Published:  November 17, 2026 at 7:14 PM Updated:  November 17, 2026 at 9:56 PM Tags:  ENOUGH , Food Safety , Recalls , USDA , FDA , Imported Food , Food Inspections , Cyclospora , Salmonella , Egg Recall , Lettuce Recall , Beef Recall , Foodborne Illness HOUSTON – Someone is supposed to be checking your food before it reaches your plate. 
 Anthony Thomas checks his own. 
 “This morning is harvest day,” Thomas said. “I’ve been raising cattle and butchering beef all my life,” he said. 
 Thomas owns ‘Thomas Cattle and Catering’ in Texas Hill County in Houston. 
 The cattle he sorts routinely head to a processing plant. What happens next, he says, is what sets his beef apart. 
 “All our beef is custom harvest, dry aged, and custom butchered, from our pasture, to your plate,” Thomas said.
 Most beef, he argues, passes through many more hands, from factories to warehouses to processing plants. That, he said, makes it “very easy for these pathogens, contaminants, diseases” to get into the meat. 
 “There’s just a problem in this country with people knowing about where their food comes from.”
 Knowing where your food comes from depends on someone checking it. On that front, the federal government is falling far short.
 Under a 2011 law, the FDA is supposed to inspect about 19,200 foreign food facilities a year. The Government Accountability Office, Congress’s watchdog, found the agency does about 900, or roughly 5%. 
 The gap comes after a summer that showed what can go wrong. 
 What foods were recalled in Texas this summer? 
 In August, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced the recall of nearly 30,000 pounds of beef imported from Argentina. It was one of many: 
 Lettuce: The CDC says 12,883 people in 21 states got sick from iceberg lettuce contaminated with cyclospora, including 24 in Texas. It was traced to Taylor Farms de Mexico. 
 Eggs: More than 19 million eggs produced in Texas, about 1.6 million dozen, were recalled over salmonella. 
 Jalapeños: Fresh peppers were pulled from shelves over salmonella. 
 Meat and poultry: Since June, the USDA has issued 17 meat and poultry recalls, seven of them involving imports, according to a review of USDA recall notices. The agency has not yet released its full 2026 summary. 
 Thomas says imports are driven by price. Companies buy meat in high volume “for the cheapest price,” he said, to “make the most amount of money.”
 What do the companies behind the recalls say? 
 Taylor Farms de Mexico (lettuce): After the FDA closed its investigation Oct. 2, the company said: “There is currently not enough evidence to conclusively determine how contamination occurred.” It said the positive sample came from wastewater outside its processing plant, collected more than three weeks after production stopped. Its central Mexico facility remains closed while it adds safety measures, and the grower where a positive sample was found is no longer a supplier. “We remain concerned for the people and families impacted by this outbreak,” the company said. 
 Midwest Poultry Services (MPS Egg Farms) (eggs): The Indiana-based company says the recall covers eggs from two of its Texas farms, sold in Texas and five nearby states, over possible salmonella contamination. It says it found the problem through its own environmental monitoring, sent eggs from the affected farms for pasteurization, and “is not distributing fresh eggs produced on its Texas farms at this time.” It advises anyone with recalled eggs to throw them away or return them for a refund. 
 Corte Argentino USA (beef): The Florida-based importer has not issued a public statement beyond the Aug. 7 USDA recall notice. 
 How many foreign food facilities does the FDA inspect? 
 Far fewer than Congress required. 
 Congress wrote the rules for how the FDA enforces food safety in the FDA Food Safety Modernization Act, signed into law in 2011.
 Lawmakers considered it the most sweeping overhaul of federal food safety standards in decades. The goal was to prevent contamination in the U.S. and abroad, rather than react after the fact.
 That shift hasn’t been easy. 
 “There’s a lot of facilities out there producing a lot of food that people are not taking a look at,” said Steve Morris, director of the Government Accountability Office’s natural resources and environment team. Morris oversees food and agriculture issues. The GAO has labeled federal food safety oversight “high risk” since 2007.
 The scale is enormous. 
 “There’s 300-plus million people, and hopefully they’re eating three times a day, right? That’s a billion servings of food daily,” Morris said.
 In January, Morris and the GAO examined whether the law’s framework is working. Among the findings:
 Targets never met: The FDA has never met its inspection targets. 
 Foreign inspections: Of the roughly 19,200 foreign inspections the law calls for each year, “the FDA was probably conducting 5% or less,” Morris said. 
 If the agency doesn’t have enough people, Morris says it should tell lawmakers. 
 “They need to go back to Congress and kind of explain that. Lay that out and say here’s what we can do with the folks we have. Here’s what we can’t do.”
 Federal cuts add to the challenge. The Trump administration announced plans to cut 20,000 employees from the Department of Health and Human Services, which works out to roughly 4,000 to 4,500 fewer FDA workers.
 What does the FDA say about the inspection gap? 
 The FDA did not make an official available for an interview but answered written questions. The agency said it “has previously reported not being adequately resourced to meet” the foreign inspection target.
 It noted that the 19,200 target applies to every registered foreign facility “regardless of the risk profile.” At the GAO’s recommendation, it is studying how many foreign inspections are actually needed to match oversight of domestic facilities, and what staffing that would take.
 The agency said it has more than 400 investigators who handle both domestic and foreign food inspections and is “actively recruiting additional staff.” 
 It did not say how many work on foreign inspections, nor did it provide inspection counts; instead, it directed readers to its public data dashboard.
 Are food recalls increasing in 2026? 
 It depends on how you count.
 Davonna Koebrick oversees Texas’ rapid-response team for foodborne illness outbreaks at the Texas Department of State Health Services. 
 “The number of recalls actually is lower than it was last year,” she said, while acknowledging there were many cases of illness.
 The federal data is less clear. Two agencies split food oversight, with the USDA covering meat, poultry and egg products and the FDA covering nearly everything else. They report recalls very differently.
 A review of raw data posted online by both agencies shows:
 FDA: Food recalls are flat to slightly up, depending on how you count. Measured by the federal budget year, they rose 18% from 2024 to 2026. 
 USDA: Meat and poultry recalls rose from 34 in 2024 to 42 in 2025, according to the agency’s annual summaries. 
 USDA, by weight: The amount of meat recalled more than tripled, to more than 71 million pounds. Most of it came from recalls due to foreign objects, such as plastic or metal. 
 Do food recalls show how many people got sick? 
 No. And they don’t prevent illness, either.
 “Recalls, by their nature, are pretty much not preventative,” Morris said. “It’s a tool that’s used once something is identified.”
 What a recall can and can’t do:
 It’s reactive. A recall happens only after a problem is found. 
 It’s mostly voluntary. “It’s basically the food manufacturers, the producers, that issue the recall when there is a food safety concern,” Morris said. The FDA can order a mandatory recall, but Morris says it hasn’t done so since 2011. 
 It doesn’t track illness. A recall pulls a product back but says nothing about who got sick, how many people or how badly. 
 Illness is also hard to count. 
 “We’re potentially talking about millions of people getting sick every year – but there’s a lot of potential underreporting of foodborne illness,” Morris said.
 No single count: The CDC doesn’t publish a single national count of foodborne illnesses each year, so there’s no clear number to set against recall counts. 
 Less tracking: The CDC’s main foodborne illness surveillance network now requires tracking for only two pathogens: salmonella and a dangerous type of E. coli known as STEC. 
 Salmonella’s toll: The CDC estimates salmonella from food sickens about 1.3 million Americans every year. CDC surveillance data shows those infections haven’t declined in years and remain above federal targets. 
 The system behind all of it is sprawling.
 “There’s basically 30 laws that govern this system,” Morris said, along with federal agencies, states, tribal entities and industry partners. “So, it’s very big. It’s very broad. It’s very complicated.”
 How do investigators trace a foodborne illness outbreak? 
 When people do get sick, Koebrick’s team in Texas works with the FDA on what’s called a traceback investigation: following contaminated food back to where it came from. 
 “We work with FDA on a daily basis,” she said. “I like to say it’s kinda like NCIS.”
 This summer’s Cyclospora outbreak shows how it works:
 Find the likely food. Investigators narrow the illnesses down to a suspected product, such as lettuce. 
 Pull records from the seller. They collect records from the restaurant or grocery store to find out who supplied the food. 
 Follow the supply chain. They track down that supplier, and the trail can lead to another state or another country. 
 Find the common source. “Eventually we start finding that common – some common suppliers,” Koebrick said. 
 The global supply chain is the challenge. 
 “There’s a large portion of our food that’s coming from somewhere else,” Morris said.
 Is locally raised beef safer than imported beef? 
 Thomas thinks so. The federal watchdog isn’t convinced.
 Back on the ranch, Thomas rides a tractor through the pasture, moving cattle from one pen to the next. “Come on, girls,” he calls.
 “We’re very transparent about our whole process,” he said. “We want people to know where their food comes from.”
 Thomas has a business interest, of course. He sells beef straight from his ranch. He’s not immune to illness, but he says his small-scale operation reduces the risk.
 Asked about that view, Morris called it “an interesting perspective.” He said the government has “a very elaborate process” for deciding whether meat is safe.
 Once foreign meat is approved, Morris said, the USDA treats it as equivalent to meat produced in the U.S. The main question for imports isn’t quality but safety: whether foreign beef could “introduce bad diseases” to the U.S.
 And Thomas concedes local ranchers can’t replace imports. Asked whether U.S. ranchers could supply all the beef sold in grocery stores, he said: “The answer is no.”
 That makes how imported meat is inspected all the more important.
 How is meat inspected in the US? 
 Domestic meat goes through its own inspection. When Thomas took his cattle for processing, he walked through the steps:
 An inspector on site: “This is a USDA-regulated plant. There is a government inspector here who makes sure everything is done to code,” Thomas said. 
 From the start: “The USDA inspector starts from the kill floor.” 
 The stamp: “That’s your U.S.D.A. inspected stamp. That means the inspector has stamped this animal safe for consumption.” 
 How do food companies prepare for inspections? 
 The paperwork, policies and procedures behind that stamp have become an industry of their own. 
 Brian Kellerman owns Kellerman Consulting, one of the companies that help food businesses get ready for government inspections. Kellerman does not work with Thomas Cattle and Catering. 
 The workload: “We tell folks to expect about a thousand hours of work for a business,” Kellerman said. 
 The rules depend on the food: “If something is going to be refrigerated, there are special requirements around temperature controls.” 
 The goal: “When the government inspector shows up, we have already worked through what those folks are going to be looking for.” 
 Most inspections happen without the public ever hearing about them. But experts agree there are holes in the inspection process.
 How can the US fix food safety inspections? 
 Morris says it starts with Congress.
 “Congress really needs to develop, for lack of a better word, kind of an overarching national strategy to guide food safety oversight,” Morris said. “You’ve got to bring everyone together. You’ve got to come up with a coordinated plan. You got to identify the goals, the leaders, the resources needed and then you go from there.”
 Thomas has his own answer. Asked what he would do if he ran the USDA or the Department of Health and Human Services, he said: “I would try to source 100 percent American beef for Americans.”
 How do I check food recalls and report food poisoning? 
 Recalls tell only part of the story, because many illnesses never get reported. Here’s what you can do:
 Check recalls: Search food recalls from both the FDA and USDA at FoodSafety.gov . 
 See a doctor: If you think something you ate made you sick, tell your doctor. 
 Report it: Report suspected food poisoning to your local health department. That’s how investigators like Koebrick find outbreaks.
